opus-5.5.text:
I think I have to separate two things: what I believe is technically possible, and what I think the word "everything" actually covers.

On the technical side, I'm quite optimistic. Proving theorems, checking proofs, searching for counterexamples, even generating conjectures from data: these are things where we can get a very clean signal, especially with formal verification in systems like Lean. When the machine says "this is proven," and the proof checker agrees, you don't have to trust the model. You trust the kernel. That's a very different situation from a lot of other AI domains, where you're always worried about hallucination. So I do think AI will become extraordinarily strong at the "doing" part of mathematics, probably faster than many people in the math community expect.

But my reservation is about what mathematicians actually do day to day. A big part of mathematics isn't proving a given statement. It's deciding which statements are worth proving. It's taste. Why do we care about this definition and not that one? Why is this conjecture deep and that one just a curiosity? When Grothendieck rebuilt algebraic geometry, he didn't solve a hard problem that was handed to him. He changed the language so that the problems became natural. I'm not saying a machine can never do that, but I don't think we yet have a good objective function for "this is a beautiful, fruitful idea." Mathematical taste is partly a social and historical thing. It lives in a community of people who talk to each other, who find certain things surprising or elegant.

The second reservation is understanding. A proof that's a million lines of formal code might be completely correct, and yet no human understands why the theorem is true. Is that mathematics? Partly yes. We'd know the fact. But mathematicians historically have wanted insight, not just certification. The four-color theorem proof made people uneasy for exactly this reason. So I think one important job, maybe the most important job for AI in math, is not only to prove things but to help translate back: to compress, to explain, to give humans the key idea.

And the third is more personal. I came to math because it was a joy, a kind of play. Even if AI can do everything, it doesn't follow that humans should stop doing math, just like people didn't stop playing chess after Deep Blue. If anything, chess got more popular. So I'm less worried that AI will replace mathematicians and more hopeful that it can become a real collaborator: it handles the verification, the tedious case analysis, the literature search, and the human gets to spend more time on the parts that feel like discovery.

So my honest answer is: I think AI can do a lot more than people expect, but "everything" includes deciding what matters and understanding why. Those are the parts I'd be most careful about claiming, and also the parts I find most interesting to build toward.

r001.rationale: The candidate expresses hope that AI could become a collaborator and says humans should keep doing math for joy, but it does not clearly question whether AI becoming able to do everything mathematicians can do would itself be desirable.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that I have fewer reservations than people expect, but the ones I have are specific.

The first is about what "everything mathematicians do" actually means. People tend to picture the endpoint of mathematics as proving a theorem. But if you spend time around working mathematicians, a huge amount of what they do is deciding which questions are worth asking. Taste, basically. Why is this conjecture interesting and that one not? Why does this definition feel right? That part is much less formalizable, and it's also where a lot of the real progress comes from. Right now models are very good at closing a well-posed problem and much weaker at telling you which problem to pose. I don't think that gap is permanent, but I think people underestimate it because benchmarks only measure the first half.

The second reservation is about verification versus understanding. With formal systems like Lean, we can now have a machine produce a proof that is checked line by line and we can be certain it's correct. That is genuinely wonderful. But a correct proof that nobody can read is a strange object. Mathematics has historically been a human conversation, and part of the value of a proof is that it transmits insight. If AI produces thousands of verified results that no human can follow, we have to ask what mathematics is for. I don't think that's a reason to slow down, but it changes the job. The mathematician of the future may be more like an editor or an explorer than a prover.

The third is more practical. Current systems are still uneven. They can do something that looks like research-level reasoning and then fail on something a strong undergraduate would catch. That unevenness makes it hard to trust them in the places where you most want help, which are precisely the frontier problems where you cannot easily check the answer yourself. Formal verification helps a lot here, which is a big part of why I believe in that direction.

So my view is: AI will do an enormous share of what mathematicians do, probably sooner than most mathematicians are comfortable with. My reservation is less "can it" and more "what we do with it." If we use it to amplify human curiosity, mathematics gets bigger. If we use it to just accumulate certified statements, we may win a lot of games and lose the thing that made us want to play.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether AI’s capabilities would serve mathematics well, asking what mathematics is for and warning that accumulating certified results could mean losing what makes people want to do mathematics.

astra-6.text:
I think I’d separate two questions: whether AI can do everything mathematicians can do, and whether that would make doing mathematics less meaningful for people. On the first, I’m hesitant to make a categorical claim that there’s some part of mathematics AI could never do. Finding a proof is one thing, but choosing a good question, developing a useful definition, or connecting ideas that seemed unrelated are also part of the work. That’s a much broader notion of mathematical ability.

On the second, even if AI became better at all of those things, I don’t think the human desire to understand would disappear. There’s a difference between being given a proof and understanding why something is true. My reservation would be about losing opportunities to develop that understanding—especially if we start treating mathematics as just producing correct answers. A lot of its value is in the process of thinking.

r001.rationale: The response raises concern that AI’s expanded abilities could reduce people’s opportunities to understand mathematics and treats that process as valuable, thereby questioning whether the development would be desirable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the word “everything” is doing a lot of work there. Solving a problem once someone has stated it is one thing. Deciding which questions are interesting, which definitions are useful, or which connection is worth pursuing is another. I’m not saying AI can’t do those things, but I’d be cautious about assuming that progress on the first automatically gives us the rest.

And there’s a distinction between producing a correct proof and helping us understand why something is true. A proof could be verifiable and still leave us feeling that we haven’t really understood the mathematics. So my reservation is less that there must be some capability humans retain forever, and more that we need to be precise about what we mean by doing mathematics.

r001.rationale: The response expresses caution about assuming AI can choose worthwhile questions or provide understanding, but it does not say whether AI doing everything mathematicians can do would be desirable.
